desc: Actinolite in elongated prismatic habit. Forms a solid solution series with tremolite (Mg-rich) and ferro-actinolite (Fe-rich). Cat's eye actinolite is known from some localities.
Classic almandine garnet displaying combined dodecahedral and trapezohedral faces. The most common garnet in metamorphic rocks, almandine is the iron-aluminium end-member of the pyralspite series.

habits.l: Prismatic with Baveno twinning and lead-green colour

note: Color from Pb+H2O color centers, not copper; often perthitic with white albite streaks
desc: Green to blue-green variety of microcline feldspar, named after the Amazon River though not actually found there. The distinctive color was long thought to result from copper, but is now attributed to lead and water in the crystal structure creating color centers. Often displays characteristic white streaks from perthitic albite intergrowths. Popular as a decorative stone and in jewelry.

note: Al2SiO5 nesosilicate; one of three Al2SiO5 polymorphs (andalusite, kyanite, sillimanite). Orthorhombic mmm; biaxial negative with 2V ~85°. Strong trichroism (X = dark red, Y = olive green, Z = orange-yellow) is primary diagnostic. Chiastolite is the carbonaceous variety showing a symmetrical cross in cross-section. Gemmological constants confirmed by Fernandes & Choudhary 2009, Gems & Gemology 45(2):120-129 (DOI 10.5741/gems.45.2.120) [VERIFIED]. Colour cause: Fe3+ substitution producing pleochroic absorption pattern. Two cleavage directions at ~90°; avoid hard impacts. Standard gem material from Brazil; chiastolite as collector's item from Spain.
desc: Coarse prismatic crystals with near-square cross-section; {110} prism dominant. Strong trichroism (red/olive-green/orange-yellow) is the diagnostic optical feature. Gem quality from Brazil (Minas Gerais). Biaxial negative with 2V ~85°.

note: Red andesine origin and treatment status frequently debated in gem trade
desc: Andesine — an intermediate plagioclase feldspar (An30-An50). Red andesine from Tibet and Oregon has become popular as a gemstone, though some material has been treated by copper diffusion.
Andradite garnet — the calcium-iron end-member of the ugrandite series. Notable for containing demantoid, the most valuable garnet variety, prized for its exceptional dispersion exceeding diamond.

habits.l: Hexagonal prism with dipyramid and pinacoid

note: Called the deceiver stone because its colours and properties mimic tourmaline, topaz, and other gems
desc: Hexagonal prism with dipyramid and pinacoid - defines hardness 5 on Mohs scale

note: Extremely high birefringence; dissolves in dilute HCl with effervescence; forms nacre in shells
desc: Calcium carbonate polymorph forming orthorhombic crystals - the less stable but higher-pressure form compared to trigonal calcite. Pseudohexagonal cyclic twins are extremely common, creating apparently hexagonal crystals. Aragonite is the primary constituent of nacre (mother-of-pearl) in mollusks and forms the skeleton of coral. Converts to calcite when heated to 400C.
Augite — the most common clinopyroxene, a major rock-forming mineral in mafic igneous rocks. Short prismatic crystals with characteristic octagonal cross-section.

habits.l: Tabular to prismatic with complex faces

note: Alters readily to malachite; reacts with dilute HCl; distinguished from lazurite by crystal form and higher SG
desc: Copper carbonate hydroxide mineral with an intense deep azure blue color that has made it prized since antiquity as a pigment (known as "mountain blue"). Unlike malachite, azurite forms well-developed prismatic crystals. The two minerals often occur together, with azurite commonly altering to malachite (pseudomorphs). Crystal specimens from Morocco and Namibia are particularly sought after.

note: Exceptionally high specific gravity (4.3-4.5) for a non-metallic mineral; used in drilling mud
desc: Tabular with complex prism faces - heavy spar, notable for high density

habits.l: Tabular to pyramidal triangular crystals; vivid blue

note: BaTiSi3O9; barium titanium cyclosilicate; hexagonal point group -6m2 (ditrigonal dipyramidal). Crystals have a triangular (not hexagonal) outline due to this point group. State gemstone of California since 1985. Primary gemmological reference: Laurs, Rohtert & Gray 1997, Gems & Gemology 33(3):166-187 (DOI 10.5741/gems.33.3.166) [VERIFIED via live API]. SWUV fluorescence mechanism confirmed by Vigier, Fritsch et al. 2023, Minerals 13(1):104 (DOI 10.3390/min13010104) [VERIFIED via live API]: colour from O2- to Ti4+ ligand-to-metal charge transfer in TiO6 groups. Fluorescence characterisation by Zhang & Shen 2023 (DOI 10.3390/min13050626) [VERIFIED]. Dispersion 0.044 is equal to diamond; confirmed per VERIFIED.md Conflict 8 (no conflict; both values accurate). RI 1.757-1.804 is above standard refractometer range; SG measurable hydrostatically.
desc: Barium titanium cyclosilicate; hexagonal point group -6m2. Crystals characteristically triangular in outline (not hexagonal). Vivid blue from O2- to Ti4+ charge transfer. Intense SWUV fluorescence is the primary field diagnostic. Only facetable gem source: San Benito County, California. Uniaxial positive; birefringence 0.047.

Beryllium aluminium silicate that produces several important gem varieties including emerald, aquamarine, morganite, heliodor, goshenite, and red beryl. Despite sharing the same basic chemistry and structure, beryl varieties differ dramatically in value based on colour, clarity, and origin. Typically forms hexagonal prismatic crystals.
Bytownite — a calcic plagioclase feldspar (An70-An90). Golden to yellow gem-quality bytownite from Mexico is occasionally faceted.

note: Also called dogtooth spar; scalenohedron has 12 scalene triangle faces
desc: Dogtooth spar — pointed scalenohedral crystals resembling canine teeth

note: Called Andean diamond in Bolivia; dispersion (0.071) is twice that of diamond; faceted gems are rare collectors items
desc: Short prismatic with dominant dipyramid - primary ore of tin

habits.l: Tabular to prismatic with multiple dome faces

note: Isostructural with barite (BaSO4); distinguished by lower SG and strontium flame test (crimson)
desc: Strontium sulfate mineral named for its characteristic celestial blue color (from Latin "caelestis" meaning heavenly). Celestine forms beautiful tabular to prismatic crystals often found in geodes. It is the primary ore of strontium, used in fireworks and flares for its crimson flame color. The world-famous celestine geodes from Madagascar can reach enormous sizes.

note: Pseudohexagonal trillings common due to cyclic twinning; cats-eye chrysoberyl is the finest chatoyant gem
desc: Tabular orthorhombic crystals often showing pseudohexagonal trillings - third hardest gemstone
Generic corundum with hexagonal prism, dipyramid and basal pinacoid - second hardest natural mineral

note: RI over refractometer limit; extremely high birefringence; contains lead - wash hands after handling
desc: Lead chromate mineral forming spectacular elongated prismatic crystals with a vivid orange-red to red color. The most highly prized mineral specimens come from Tasmania, Australia, where crystals can reach lengths of 10+ cm. Named from Greek "krokos" (saffron) for its color. Despite its beauty, crocoite is too soft and fragile for jewelry use.

note: RI over refractometer limit; extremely high SG aids identification
desc: Copper oxide mineral forming deep red octahedral crystals with exceptional adamantine lustre. Cuprite has one of the highest refractive indices of any gemstone (2.848), exceeding diamond. Rare transparent crystals from the now-depleted Onganja mine in Namibia are highly prized collector gems. Too soft for jewelry use but stunning as cabinet specimens.

habits.l: Nested growth — green phantom inside octahedron

desc: Octahedron with minor dodecahedron truncation and dense triangular trigon etch pits on {111} faces

habits.l: Short prismatic; vivid green from Cr3+

colors.c: White to grey four-rayed star in reflected light

desc: Calcium-magnesium pyroxene forming short prismatic crystals with characteristic near-90-degree cleavage angles. Chrome diopside from Russia displays intense emerald-green color rivaling tsavorite and is an important gemstone. Star diopside with four-rayed asterism is also known. The violan variety shows attractive violet-blue color.
Dravite — the magnesium-bearing tourmaline end-member. Named after the Drava river area in Austria. Brown to yellowish-brown colour; occasionally produces attractive orange-brown gems.
Elbaite — the lithium-bearing tourmaline species producing most gem-quality tourmaline. Named after Elba island, Italy. Includes rubellite, indicolite, verdelite, achroite, and Paraíba varieties.

colors.c: Brownish-green to bronze-coloured with metallic schiller
Pale grey to pale green, yellowish-brown

desc: Enstatite — the magnesium end-member of the orthopyroxene series. Gem varieties include chrome-green enstatite and bronzite with its submetallic bronze schiller.

note: Variable birefringence depending on iron content; high relief in thin section
desc: Calcium-aluminum-iron silicate forming elongated prismatic crystals, typically striated parallel to the b-axis. Epidote displays a distinctive pistachio to yellowish-green color (the "epidote green") and is strongly pleochroic. While occasionally faceted as a collector gem, its perfect cleavage and strong pleochroism make cutting challenging.

habits.l: Interpenetrating twin with cube and octahedron

note: Fluorite is the mineral that gives its name to the phenomenon of fluorescence
desc: Perfect cubic habit — defines hardness 4 on Mohs scale

note: Opaque mineral; exceptionally high SG due to lead content; toxic - wash hands after handling
desc: Lead sulfide mineral displaying perfect cubic cleavage - the type example of cubic cleavage in mineralogy. Galena has a brilliant metallic lustre when fresh but tarnishes to dull grey. It is the primary ore of lead and an important source of silver. The combination of high density, perfect cleavage, and metallic lustre makes it easily identifiable.
Grossular garnet — the calcium-aluminium member of the ugrandite series. Produces several important gem varieties including tsavorite (green) and hessonite (orange).

note: Can be scratched with fingernail; slightly soluble in water; dehydrates to anhydrite when heated
desc: Hydrated calcium sulfate - one of the softest minerals used as a hardness standard. Gypsum forms large tabular crystals, often with characteristic swallowtail twinning. The giant gypsum crystals of the Naica Mine in Mexico (up to 12 meters long) are among the largest crystals ever found. Varieties include transparent selenite, fibrous satin spar, and fine- grained alabaster.

note: Soluble in water; hygroscopic - must be stored in dry conditions; characteristic salty taste
desc: Common salt - the naturally occurring mineral form of sodium chloride. Halite forms perfect cubic crystals with three directions of cleavage at right angles. Best known for its distinctive taste (though taste testing is discouraged). Blue halite, colored by radiation-induced F-centers, is particularly prized by collectors.

habits.l: Rounded dodecahedral to irregular; vivid violet-blue

note: Sodium calcium aluminosilicate sulfate; cubic -43m; sodalite group member. Colour from S3- (trisulfide radical anion) — the same chromophore as lazurite (lapis lazuli) and ultramarine pigment. Confirmed by Farsang, Caracas et al. 2023, American Mineralogist 108:2234-2243 (DOI 10.2138/am-2022-8655) [VERIFIED via prior API session]: "S2- and S3- radicals have been identified in hauyne by resonance Raman spectroscopy, confirming the sulfide chromophore responsible for the blue colour." Sodalite-group structural context confirmed by Chukanov et al. 2020, Minerals 10:363 (DOI 10.3390/min10040363) [VERIFIED]. Gemmological constants (SG, RI) from Read 7th ed. (DOI 10.4324/9780080507224) [PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED]. Very low SG 2.40-2.50 is the key physical separator from virtually all other blue gems. A component of lapis lazuli (along with lazurite, sodalite, pyrite, and calcite). Extremely rare as a faceted gem; primarily collector's gem.
desc: Sodium calcium aluminium silicate sulfate; cubic -43m; sodalite group. Vivid violet-blue from S3- radical anion chromophore (same as lazurite). Very low SG 2.40-2.50 is the key physical diagnostic. Extremely small faceted stones; primarily a collector's gem. Eifel district (Germany) is the primary gem-quality source.

habits.l: Tabular to platy crystals; massive specularite

note: Fe2O3; trigonal -3m; isostructural with corundum (Al2O3). Red streak is diagnostic despite metallic grey appearance. RI not measurable on refractometer (opaque). Non-magnetic — contrast with hematine (pressed iron powder simulant, strongly attracted to neodymium magnet). Castroviejo (2023) mineralogical reference (DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-12654-3_60) [VERIFIED] confirms crystal system, chemistry, and oxide group classification. SG and hardness from Read 7th ed. (DOI 10.4324/9780080507224) [PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED]. Gem material is the specular silvery variety (specularite); kidney ore is botryoidal. Hematine (synthetic/pressed) is the common simulant — detected by strong magnetism.
desc: Gem-quality hematite as specularite — massive compact material with mirror-like metallic lustre. In crystal form: rhombohedral or tabular plates on {0001}; also botryoidal (kidney ore). Red streak is the single most important diagnostic feature.
Rare crystalline jadeite showing monoclinic prismatic habit. Individual crystals are rarely seen; jadeite occurs almost exclusively as interlocking aggregates.

note: Mg-Al-Fe boroaluminosilicate; orthorhombic mmm; complex formula with IMA species kornerupine (<=0.5 B per formula unit) and prismatine (>0.5 B; separate IMA species since 1997). Optical constants and cat's-eye kornerupine from Sri Lanka confirmed by Zwaan 1996, Gems & Gemology 32(4):262-269 (DOI 10.5741/gems.32.4.262) [VERIFIED]. Elahera gem field confirmed by Gunawardene & Rupasinghe 1986 (DOI 10.5741/gems.22.2.80) [VERIFIED]. Gem localities by Shigley et al. 2000 (DOI 10.5741/gems.36.4.292) [VERIFIED]. Strong trichroism (green/yellow/red-brown) is the primary field diagnostic; "immediately recognisable under the dichroscope." Colour cause: Fe2+ (green); Cr3+ in intensely green stones. Cat's-eye variety: fibrous hollow tubes parallel to c-axis.
desc: Orthorhombic Mg-Al boroaluminosilicate; elongated prismatic habit. Strong trichroism (green/yellow/red-brown) visible in dichroscope is the primary diagnostic. Sri Lanka and Madagascar are the main gem sources. Biaxial negative.

note: Diagnostic variable hardness; often contains color zoning; parting on {001}; good toughness despite cleavage
desc: Aluminum silicate polymorph (with andalusite and sillimanite) famous for its extreme directional hardness variation - hardness 4-5 parallel to the c-axis but 6-7 perpendicular to it. This anisotropy makes kyanite challenging to cut but is diagnostic. The classic blue color derives from iron and titanium, though green, orange, and colorless varieties exist. Often color-zoned.

Plagioclase feldspar displaying labradorescence - striking plays of colour including blue, green, gold, and purple caused by light interference from lamellar twinning. The colours appear in patches or broad flashes and are best seen on specific crystal orientations. Finnish labradorite showing the full spectral range is marketed as "Spectrolite."

note: Well-crystallized specimens extremely rare; usually occurs massive in lapis lazuli rock
desc: Well-formed dodecahedral crystals of lazurite are extremely rare. When found, they show rhombic dodecahedron habit with minor cube. Crystal specimens are highly prized by collectors and come primarily from the Badakhshan mines in Afghanistan.

note: Opaque mineral - RI not measurable with standard equipment; strongly magnetic
desc: Strongly magnetic iron oxide mineral forming perfect octahedral crystals. One of the most magnetic of all naturally-occurring minerals on Earth. Magnetite is opaque with a metallic to sub-metallic lustre and is the primary ore of iron. Its strong magnetism is diagnostic - crystals will attract iron filings and deflect a compass needle.

note: Crystal specimens extremely rare and valuable; vast majority of malachite is massive/botryoidal
desc: Well-formed prismatic crystals of malachite are extremely rare and highly prized by collectors. When found, they typically show short prismatic habit with multiple pinacoid and prism faces. Crystal specimens command high premiums over massive material.

habits.l: Massive aggregate; vivid green with black chromite inclusions

chem: Multi-mineral rock aggregate; dominant phases kosmochlor (NaCrSi2O6) + jadeite (NaAlSi2O6) + albite (NaAlSi3O8) + chromite (FeCr2O4)
note: Multi-mineral decorative rock; NOT a single IMA mineral species. Dominant mineralogy: kosmochlor (NaCrSi2O6, a chromium pyroxene, monoclinic 2/m) + jadeite (NaAlSi2O6, monoclinic 2/m) + albite + chromite. Crystal system assigned as monoclinic (dominant pyroxene phase). First described by Gübelin 1965, Journal of Gemmology (DOI 10.15506/jog.1965.9.10.329) [VERIFIED]. Mineralogical composition confirmed by Harlow et al. 2000 (DOI 10.15506/jog.2000.27.2.87) [VERIFIED] and Ou Yang et al. 2025 (DOI 10.3390/cryst15110983) [VERIFIED]. CAUTION: This is a polycrystalline multi-mineral rock aggregate — RI, SG, and hardness are composite values depending on the mix of phases. The Chelsea filter red reaction is from Cr3+ in kosmochlor. Often confused with jadeite but the chromite spots and higher Cr content distinguish it. Not a standard jade variety.
desc: Polycrystalline multi-mineral rock (kosmochlor + jadeite + albite + chromite) from Kachin State, Myanmar. Vivid emerald-green matrix with black to dark green chromite spots. CDL represents the dominant monoclinic pyroxene (kosmochlor/jadeite) phase as proxy for the aggregate. Not an IMA mineral species; included as gem material per FGA/Diploma curriculum coverage.

note: BeMg2Al6O12; hexagonal, rhombohedral, point group -3m. IMA revised name: magnesiotaaffeite-6N'3S per Armbruster 2002 (DOI 10.1127/0935-1221/2002/0014-0389) [VERIFIED via live API]. ATR-FTIR and Raman distinction from taaffeite confirmed by Thongnopkun 2024 (DOI 10.1016/j.vibspec.2024.103733) [VERIFIED via live API]: "ATR-FTIR and Raman spectroscopy efficiently distinguish musgravite from taaffeite using diagnostic vibrational band positions." Higher RI (1.719-1.736) and SG (3.61-3.68) than taaffeite (RI 1.717-1.730, SG 3.60-3.62) but ranges overlap; FTIR/Raman is definitive. Colour cause: Cr, Fe or V substitution (not firmly established for all colours; per VERIFIED.md REJ-07, do not present as confirmed fact). Type locality: Musgrave Ranges, South Australia; fewer than 10 faceted stones known before 2000. Note: musgravite is a separate IMA species from taaffeite, not merely a variety.
desc: BeMg2Al6O12; hexagonal (trigonal rhombohedral). One of the rarest faceted gem minerals. Birefringent (uniaxial negative); distinguishes from spinel (isotropic) on polariscope. Separated from taaffeite by FTIR/Raman; slightly higher RI and SG but ranges overlap. Type locality: Musgrave Ranges, South Australia (1967).

note: CAUTION - contains arsenic; extremely high birefringence; handle with care; wash hands after handling
desc: Arsenic trisulfide mineral with a bright lemon-yellow to golden-orange color and pearly lustre on cleavage surfaces. The name derives from Latin "auripigmentum" (gold pigment) - orpiment was used historically as a yellow pigment despite its toxicity. Perfect cleavage produces thin, flexible but inelastic sheets. Often found with realgar.

Potassium feldspar (K-feldspar) forming prismatic monoclinic crystals, often in granite and pegmatite. The name refers to the nearly 90-degree cleavage angle (Greek "orthos" = right, "klasis" = breaking). Orthoclase is the host mineral for moonstone (with albite exsolution) and includes the transparent yellow variety known as noble orthoclase.

habits.l: Short prismatic with lily pad inclusions

desc: Short prismatic with wedge terminations and diagnostic lily pad (discoid) inclusions

note: Albite twinning striations visible on {010} cleavage distinguish plagioclase from orthoclase
desc: Polysynthetic lamellar twinning on {010}, the most common twinning in plagioclase feldspars. Albite law twins form parallel sets of thin lamellae that create characteristic striations visible on crystal faces and cleavage surfaces. These striations are a key diagnostic feature for identifying plagioclase. The composition plane is {010} with twin axis perpendicular to it.

note: Called fool's gold due to superficial resemblance to gold; much lighter (SG 5 vs 19.3) and harder than gold
desc: Cubic habit with characteristic striated faces — the most common sulfide mineral
Pyrope garnet — the magnesium end-member of the pyralspite series. The name derives from Greek 'pyropos' meaning fire-like, referring to its deep red colour. Classic Bohemian garnets are pyrope.
Hexagonal prism with rhombohedral terminations and horizontal striations on prism faces — most abundant mineral in Earth's crust

habits.l: Short prismatic with multiple dome forms

note: CAUTION - contains arsenic; degrades to pararealgar in light; store in darkness; wash hands after handling
desc: Arsenic sulfide mineral with a distinctive red to orange-red color, also known as "ruby sulfur." Realgar forms striking prismatic crystals often striated parallel to the c-axis. It is light-sensitive and gradually degrades to yellow pararealgar powder upon prolonged exposure to light. Museum specimens must be stored in darkness. Contains arsenic - handle with care.

note: Extremely high birefringence; dissolves in warm dilute HCl with effervescence; too soft for ring use
desc: Manganese carbonate mineral prized for its rose-pink to deep red color. The "Alma King" from Colorado's Sweet Home Mine is considered one of the finest mineral specimens ever found. Well-formed rhombohedral crystals are highly sought but rare.

habits.l: Tabular to prismatic, pink with black manganese oxide veins

note: Rose-red colour from Mn2+; black veining from manganese oxide alteration; official gem of Massachusetts
desc: Manganese inosilicate - rose-red colour with characteristic black manganese oxide veins

note: Extreme birefringence (0.287) and dispersion (0.330) - among highest of any mineral; synthetic rutile once used as diamond simulant (Titania)
desc: Elongated prismatic habit - the most common natural form of TiO2

note: High-temperature polymorph; orthoclase is the medium-temperature equivalent
desc: Sanidine — the high-temperature polymorph of potassium feldspar found in volcanic rocks. Sometimes displays a glassy transparency prized by collectors. Carlsbad twinning is very common.

note: Na-Ca aluminosilicate solid solution series (marialite to meionite); tetragonal 4/m. Yellow scapolite from Madagascar confirmed by Superchi et al. 2010, Gems & Gemology 46(4):274-279 (DOI 10.5741/gems.46.4.274) [VERIFIED]. Cat's-eye and unusual properties from Sri Lanka confirmed by Zwaan 1996, Gems & Gemology 32(4):262-269 (DOI 10.5741/gems.32.4.262) [VERIFIED]. Colour cause in yellow stones: colour centres (F-centres; not transition metal ions) — Fritsch & Rossman 1988 (DOI 10.5741/gems.24.1.3) [VERIFIED]. Strong LWUV fluorescence (yellow-orange) is a key diagnostic. Two prismatic cleavage directions complicate faceting.
desc: Tetragonal prismatic crystals; Na-Ca aluminosilicate solid-solution series (marialite–meionite). Strong LWUV fluorescence in yellow material is diagnostic. Cat's-eye variety from Myanmar (Burma) is most prized. Uniaxial negative optic character.

note: Trace molybdenum shifts fluorescence to yellowish-green; important tungsten ore
desc: Calcium tungstate mineral known for its brilliant blue-white fluorescence under shortwave UV light - one of the most spectacular fluorescent minerals. Scheelite forms dipyramidal crystals with high lustre approaching diamond. While occasionally faceted for collectors, its softness and distinct cleavage make it unsuitable for jewelry wear.

colors.c: Grey-green to mottled green, white, pale bluish-green

note: Principal IMA-approved gem species is antigorite (monoclinic 2/m); lizardite is trigonal (-3m) — both formula Mg3Si2O5(OH)4 with Mg:Fe and Cr substitution. Gem material is invariably polycrystalline massive aggregate; crystal system given for the dominant antigorite (bowenite) phase. Chrysotile (fibrous asbestiform variety) is NOT used as gem material. Chemical formula and mineral group confirmed by Ross & Shannon 1962, USGS Professional Paper 384-A (DOI 10.3133/pp384a) [VERIFIED]. RI and SG from Read 7th ed. (DOI 10.4324/9780080507224) [PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED]. Serpentine as jade simulant ("New jade" trade name) documented by Hobbs 1982, Gems & Gemology (DOI 10.5741/gems.18.1.3) [VERIFIED]. Trade name "New jade" is misleading; material is not jadeite or nephrite.
desc: Bowenite variety of antigorite; translucent apple-green massive aggregate with waxy lustre. Polycrystalline — CDL represents the dominant antigorite phase. Used as jade simulant but easily distinguished by low RI, SG, and hardness.

note: MgAlBO4; orthorhombic mmm; olivine-structure type borate. Named from Sinhala (= Sri Lanka). Formally described as a distinct mineral species in 1952; previously confused with brown peridot. Key distinction from peridot: biaxial negative optic sign (peridot is biaxial positive); higher SG 3.46-3.50 (peridot 3.27-3.37). Sri Lanka alluvial occurrence confirmed by Zwaan 1982, Gems & Gemology 18(2):62-71 (DOI 10.5741/gems.18.2.62) [VERIFIED] and Shigley et al. 2000 (DOI 10.5741/gems.36.4.292) [VERIFIED]. Constants from Read 7th ed. (DOI 10.4324/9780080507224) [PARTIALLY_SUPPORTED].
desc: Orthorhombic borate with olivine-type structure. Pale yellow-brown to brownish-green gem. Biaxial negative (key distinction from biaxial positive peridot). Sri Lanka alluvials are the primary source. High birefringence (0.038) produces visible doubling in deeper stones.

note: Well-formed crystals uncommon; sodalite usually occurs as massive aggregates
desc: Well-formed dodecahedral crystals of sodalite are rare. When found, they show rhombic dodecahedron habit with minor cube truncation. Most gem-quality sodalite is massive material.

Manganese aluminium garnet known for its vibrant orange to reddish-orange colours. Fine vivid orange specimens are marketed as "Mandarin" or "Fanta" garnet. Nigerian material is particularly prized for its intense orange saturation. Forms a solid solution series with pyrope and almandine.

habits.l: Characteristic wedge shape with extreme dispersion

note: Dispersion exceeds diamond; high birefringence causes visible facet doubling; too soft for everyday wear
desc: Calcium titanium silicate forming characteristic wedge or envelope-shaped crystals (Greek "sphenos" = wedge). Sphene possesses the highest dispersion of any common gemstone (0.051), exceeding even diamond (0.044), producing exceptional fire in well-cut stones. Combined with strong pleochroism and high birefringence, sphene displays remarkable optical effects but is challenging to cut due to its softness and distinct cleavage.
Octahedral habit with diagnostic octahedral inclusions (negative crystals)

habits.l: Elongated prismatic with strong pink pleochroism

desc: Spodumene — a lithium pyroxene that produces the gem varieties kunzite (pink-violet) and hiddenite (chrome-green). Known for its perfect cleavage which makes cutting challenging.

note: More rare than 60-degree twins; highly sought by collectors
desc: Cruciform penetration twin at 90 degrees, forming a perfect cross or plus-sign shape. Also called "St. Andrew's cross" or "Greek cross" due to its symmetrical cruciform shape. Rarer and more prized than the 60-degree twins. The name staurolite derives from the Greek "stauros" meaning cross.

Plagioclase feldspar displaying aventurescence - a glittery, metallic reflection from included reflective platelets. Oregon sunstone is unique in containing copper platelets rather than the hematite or goethite found in other sources. Oregon material can also show strong dichroism and occur in transparent gem-quality crystals. Some specimens display bicolour or tricolour zoning.

habits.l: Rounded to subhedral from alluvial reworking

note: BeMgAl4O8; hexagonal, rhombohedral subgroup, point group -3m. IMA revised name: magnesiotaaffeite-2N'2S per Armbruster 2002 (DOI 10.1127/0935-1221/2002/0014-0389) [VERIFIED via live API]. Gemmological constants and analytical identification confirmed by Thongnopkun 2024 (DOI 10.1016/j.vibspec.2024.103733) [VERIFIED via live API]. CRITICAL DIAGNOSTIC NOTE (per VERIFIED.md Conflict 7 + flag F-05): Doubly refractive (uniaxial negative) — this is the primary and immediate separation from spinel (isotropic). SG 3.60-3.62 overlaps spinel (3.58-3.65); SG alone is NOT sufficient for separation. RI 1.717-1.730 also overlaps with some spinel specimens. The polariscope (DR test) is the definitive field separation. ATR-FTIR and Raman distinguish taaffeite from musgravite (magnesiotaaffeite-6N'3S) by vibrational band positions. Musgravite: higher SG ~3.61-3.68, higher RI ~1.723-1.736; see separate musgravite.yaml entry. Historical note: Edward Taaffe purchased the original stone in a Dublin gem dealer's parcel in 1945, believing it spinel; the double refraction was noticed and confirmed as a new species in 1951. Gem localities confirmed by Shigley et al. 2000 (DOI 10.5741/gems.36.4.292) [VERIFIED].
desc: One of the rarest gem minerals; BeMgAl4O8; hexagonal (trigonal rhombohedral symmetry). Birefringent (uniaxial negative) unlike isotropic spinel — polariscope DR test is the primary separation. Most gem material is alluvially reworked (Sri Lanka, Myanmar). FTIR/Raman required to distinguish from musgravite (magnesiotaaffeite-6N'3S).
Prismatic zoisite variety

Schorl — the iron-bearing tourmaline end-member and the most common tourmaline species. Black colour from high iron content. The most abundant boron mineral.
Tremolite — the magnesian end-member of the tremolite-actinolite series. Fibrous varieties constitute nephrite jade. Named after Val Tremola in the Swiss Alps.

note: Extremely rare crystal form; the vast majority of turquoise is cryptocrystalline massive
desc: Well-formed triclinic crystals of turquoise are extremely rare. When found, they occur as tiny prismatic to tabular crystals rarely exceeding a few millimetres. The vast majority of turquoise is cryptocrystalline massive material.
Uvarovite — the rarest garnet end-member, a vivid emerald-green chromium garnet. Typically found as small drusy crystals on chromite ore, rarely large enough for faceting. Named after Count Uvarov.

note: Named by Werner in 1795 for crystals from Mount Vesuvius; gemologists often use the older name idocrase

desc: Lead molybdate mineral forming characteristically thin, tabular, square crystals with brilliant orange to red colors and adamantine lustre. The thin crystal habit and exceptional color saturation make wulfenite one of the most prized collector minerals. Crystals from the Red Cloud Mine in Arizona are particularly famous for their vivid red color.
